Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when cash moves. If you do work in January but aren’t paid until March, accrual accounting shows the income in January. If you get a bill for supplies used in January but pay it later, the expense is recorded in January. That way each period shows the activities that actually took place.

Cash-basis accounting records income and expenses only when money is received or paid. Using the same examples, income wouldn’t appear until March and the supplies expense wouldn’t show until you pay the bill. Cash basis is simpler and can be easier for very small operations, but it can make results look uneven — big payments can make one month look excellent and the next look poor even if work was steady. In short: accrual follows when things happen; cash basis follows when money changes hands.
